To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the models recently used to prove the superiority of ResNets are actually different from the standard ResNets and (ii) the models recently proposed to outperform ResNet are indeed a different model, and they have a better representation guarantee than ResNets.

1) ResNEst is a model that is different from ResNets; 2) A-ResNEsts are ResNEsts that are guaranteed to have no worse performance with additional blocks; 3) ResNEsts are not as powerful as DenseNEsts.

(a) the ResNEst is a basis function model with a coupling problem between basis learning and linear estimation, (b) the A-ResNEsts decouple the basis learning from linear estimation, (c) A-ResNESTs have desirable properties of no worse performance with adding a block, (d) any DenseNEst is represented as a ResNEst, and (e) any DenseNEsts exhibit no worse performance with additional blocks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (i) What are the limitations of ResNets? (ii) How can we improve ResNets to overcome such limitations?
a new class of DNN models, ResNEsts and DenseNets, that have improved representation properties and can be used to prove lower bounds on generalization errors of standard ResNets and DenseNets.
a fundamental question: What is a good ResNet architecture? Our results suggest that the key to answering this question is the number of basis elements.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in order to achieve the desirable property, a ResNet must have a sufficiently wide input space.
the models considered in the literature proving ResNets are better than linear estimators are not ResNets but ResNEsts, which are a special class of ResNets that are not used widely in practice.
the recent literature proving ResNets are better than linear prediction is actually about a different class of models, i.e., DenseNEsts or ResNEsts, and not ResNets.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

ResNEsts can be viewed as the most basic form of ResNets that can be used to prove the above-mentioned property, while DenseNEsts are the best form of ResNests in terms of the desirable property and the empirical performance.
ResNets can be improved by simply dropping nonlinear functions at the final residual representations, and the resulting ResNEst can be improved further by densely connecting the residual blocks.
we show the difference between ResNEsts and DenseNets, and we propose DenseNEsts, which are different from both ResNEsts and ResNets.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the coupling between basis learning and linear estimation in ResNets is not only a problem of diminishing features, but also a problem of feature reuse.
the desirable properties of ResNets can be achieved with a different architectural design, i.e., the design of ResNEsts or DenseNEsts.
, to achieve the desirable training property of ResNets, the key is not only to use a block-based architecture, but also to carefully design the block structure to decouple the coupling problem.
